title: Kunal Bahl's 2007 H-1B Rejection at Microsoft Led Him to Build Snapdeal
excerpt: The Snapdeal and Titan Capital co-founder recounts how a rejected petition in 2007 ended his Microsoft plan and started his company, incorporated days before he landed in India.
body:
• Kunal Bahl, who co-founded Snapdeal and the investment firm Titan Capital, has recalled in a Business Insider essay how his H-1B petition was rejected in June or July 2007, while he was working at Microsoft in the United States.
  • Microsoft suggested he work from its India office and try again for the H-1B after a year. He decided instead to return to India and work for himself.
  • He and his school friend Rohit Bansal incorporated their company on September 12, 2007, days before Bahl landed in India, starting with a physical coupon-book business funded by about $60,000 of pooled savings.
  • For readers in the H-1B process today, Bahl's account is a reminder that a rejected petition ends that application, not a career: his employer's fallback was an India-office transfer and a fresh attempt a year later. Current rules are on the USCIS H-1B page.

Kunal Bahl is the co-founder of Snapdeal and of Titan Capital, and a judge on Shark Tank India. In an as-told-to essay published by Business Insider, he has described how the business career that followed began with a rejection: in 2007, while he was working at Microsoft in the United States, his H-1B petition was turned down, and the company told him he would have to return to India if he wanted to stay with it.

Bahl, now 43, leads AceVector Limited, the Indian digital commerce holding company, and Titan Capital, the investment firm he runs with Rohit Bansal. His account, reported this week by India Today, is a retrospective, not a new visa case. The rejection happened nearly two decades ago. What makes it current is Bahl's argument, made to readers facing immigration struggles now, that the India he returned to in 2007 and the India a founder returns to today are different countries.

The rejection

Bahl grew up in New Delhi and went to the University of Pennsylvania for a program that blended an engineering and a business degree. He interned at Microsoft during his junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating. He was on an F-1 visa, working under Optional Practical Training, the temporary work authorization after graduation, and counting down the days until it expired while he waited for the H-1B outcome. The H-1B program allows US employers to employ foreign workers in specialty occupations; the process then, as now, ran through the employer, as the USCIS cap-season guidance sets out for current applicants.

"I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected," Bahl says in the essay. It was, he says, unfathomable to him at first that a petition from a company like Microsoft would not be approved. He checked with the Microsoft team and gathered from their faces that there was a finality to the rejection.

The choice

Microsoft's offer, as Bahl recounts it, was to work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year. He had not considered moving back to India. His decision was narrower than a rejection of the company: if he was going back to his own country, he would work for himself, not for Microsoft. He says he felt liberated, in one respect, because he no longer had to figure out the H-1B situation or worry about visas and green cards.

"In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time."

— Kunal Bahl, in his Business Insider essay

He called Rohit Bansal, his best friend from high school, who was working in a financial institution. The two had talked in class about starting a business together. Their company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before Bahl touched down in India.

Building in the India of 2007

The India Bahl returned to had, in his telling, very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments that were few and far between. Starting a company was frowned upon. The venture began as a physical coupon-book business. Angel investors were not common, so the seed capital was the pair's own: about $60,000 pooled from a year of corporate jobs, while they lived with their families and worked from a small basement office in Delhi.

The company pivoted from online couponing to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, Snapdeal. Bahl says two publicly listed companies have since been spun off from the original coupon-book business. In 2011, once they had built up capital, the pair began investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital. Over the last 15 years, Bahl says, they have invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public.

What he says to founders facing the same letter

Bahl is careful, in the essay, about the limits of his own story. It was easy for him to pack up and come back because he was not married and did not have children, and he says he knows it is far more difficult for workers who have dependents living with them in the US, such as children or parents. He says he empathizes with workers facing immigration struggles in the US.

His closing argument is about what changed on the Indian side. India now has a billion internet users, ubiquitous smartphones, coworking spaces, dense talent and a robust funding ecosystem, in his account. "There is no better time to come back to India," he says. That is one founder's judgment, offered from a career the rejection set in motion.
